nodes.label: Right-Triangle Trigonometric Ratios and Special Angles
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in right-triangle geometry (the Pythagorean theorem, angle sum of a triangle, AA similarity and side-length proportions, and the 30°-60°-90° and 45°-45°-90° special right triangles) together with basic radical simplification. Defines the six trigonometric ratios—sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent—for an acute angle θ in a right triangle via opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse lengths, using AA similarity as the key bridge proving that each ratio depends only on θ and not on triangle scale. Establishes the basic reciprocal definitions (csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ), quotient relations (tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, cot θ = cos θ / sin θ), and complementary-angle cofunction pairs (sin(90° − θ) = cos θ, tan(90° − θ) = cot θ, sec(90° − θ) = csc θ) directly from swapping the two acute angles of a right triangle. Derives and internalizes exact trigonometric values for 30°, 45°, and 60° from unit-scaled special triangles, and trains recovering all six exact ratios of an acute angle from a single given ratio by constructing a labeled right triangle and applying the Pythagorean theorem. Explicitly guards against confusing opposite/adjacent sides when the reference vertex changes or mistaking csc θ for 1/cos θ. Enables the learner to compute exact acute-angle trigonometric ratios and reconstruct all six ratios from one given value. Leaves solving for unknown angles or sides in applications, non-acute angles, radian measure, and algebraic identity proofs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Angles in Standard Position and Radian Measure
nodes.explanation: Assumes secondary entry background in degree angle measure, circle circumference C = 2πr, proportional reasoning, and plotting points in the four Cartesian quadrants. Introduces directed angles in standard position (vertex at the origin, initial ray along the positive x-axis, counterclockwise rotation positive and clockwise rotation negative), quadrantal angles, and coterminal angles (θ + 360°k or θ + 2πk for integers k), contrasting geometrically identical terminal rays with distinct amounts of rotation. Defines radian measure as the dimensionless central-angle ratio θ = s/r of intercepted arc length to radius, proving via circle similarity that the ratio is independent of r and establishing 180° = π radians (1 rad ≈ 57.3°). Builds fluent exact degree-radian conversion—both procedurally via multiplying by π/180° or 180°/π and structurally as fractions of π (multiples of π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2)—along with locating the quadrant of any positive or negative angle and finding its least nonnegative coterminal angle in [0, 2π) or [0°, 360°). Highlights the common misconception that π itself is an angle in degrees rather than π radians ≈ 3.1416 rad. Enables the learner to sketch arbitrary directed angles in degrees or radians, convert cleanly between angle units, and classify terminal rays and coterminal families. Leaves arc-length and sector-area calculations and trigonometric function values to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Arc Length and Sector Area in Radian Measure
nodes.explanation: Builds on radian measure and assumes basic circle area A = πr² to develop circular measurement formulas that operate natively in radians. Derives arc length s = rθ directly from the radian definition θ = s/r and derives circular sector area A = ½r²θ (and A = ½rs) by proportionality with the full circle area (θ / 2π = A / πr²). Emphasizes the critical unit condition that θ must be expressed in radians—diagnosing the frequent error of substituting degree measures directly into s = rθ or A = ½r²θ—and solves both direct and inverse measurement problems (finding s, r, θ, or A from two given quantities, including compound regions such as circular rings and sectors). Enables the learner to compute arc lengths, central angles, radii, and sector areas accurately in applied geometry problems (such as latitude arc distances, pendulums, and windshield wipers). Leaves angular/linear speed kinematics to an optional enrichment lesson and trigonometric values to the unit-circle branch.

nodes.label: Angular Speed, Linear Speed, and Circular Motion
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment building on arc length in radians (and assuming unit conversions and constant-rate motion v = d/t) to analyze uniform circular motion. Defines constant angular speed ω = θ/t (in radians per unit time) and tangential linear speed v = s/t, substituting s = rθ to derive the kinematic bridge v = rω. Trains converting fluently between revolutions per minute (rpm), degrees per second, and radians per second (using 1 rev = 2π rad), and applies v = rω to wheels rolling without slipping, rotating blades, and coupled belt-driven or meshed gears (distinguishing same-axle components that share ω from belt- or tooth-coupled rims that share v). Enables the learner to compute angular and linear speeds across coupled rotational systems without introducing calculus or vector kinematics.

nodes.label: Solving Right Triangles and Applied Measurement
nodes.explanation: Builds on acute right-triangle trigonometric ratios to solve any right triangle completely given either one side and one acute angle or two sides. Explicitly supplies calculator trigonometric evaluation and inverse-ratio lookup (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹) solely as numerical tools for recovering the unique acute angle in (0°, 90°) from a known positive ratio, noting that the formal theory of inverse trigonometric functions and restricted domains belongs to Trigonometric Identities and Equations. Trains selecting the most direct ratio to avoid propagating rounded intermediate values, checking answers for geometric reasonableness (hypotenuse longest, angle sum 90° for acute angles), and translating verbal geometry into labeled right-triangle models—covering angles of elevation and depression (stressing that both are measured from the horizontal, not the vertical), compass bearings, and multi-triangle indirect measurement problems (such as finding tower height from two sighting positions along a baseline). Enables the learner to solve right triangles and applied surveying/navigation problems reliably, leaving oblique triangles to the Laws of Sines and Cosines.

nodes.label: The Unit Circle Definition of Sine and Cosine
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes acute right-triangle ratios and angles in standard position with radian measure to extend sine and cosine from acute angles to all real numbers. Defines cos t = x and sin t = y for any real input t via the terminal point P(x, y) reached by wrapping arc length |t| (counterclockwise for t ≥ 0, clockwise for t < 0) around the unit circle x² + y² = 1 from (1, 0), and verifies consistency with right-triangle ratios when 0 < t < π/2 by dropping a perpendicular to the x-axis. Develops the reference-angle and coordinate-symmetry bridge—reflecting first-quadrant special points (π/6, π/4, π/3) and quadrantal points (0, π/2, π, 3π/2) across the axes—to evaluate exact values of sin t and cos t at any integer multiple of π/6 or π/4 without rote table memorization. Establishes immediate geometric consequences directly from the circle: the Pythagorean relation cos² t + sin² t = 1, boundedness −1 ≤ sin t ≤ 1 and −1 ≤ cos t ≤ 1, 2π-periodicity (sin(t + 2π) = sin t, cos(t + 2π) = cos t), supplementary-angle relations (sin(π − t) = sin t, cos(π − t) = −cos t), and even/odd symmetry (cos(−t) = cos t, sin(−t) = −sin t). Enables the learner to evaluate exact sine and cosine values for arbitrary special real inputs and deduce quadrant signs and symmetries geometrically. Leaves the remaining four functions, general circles of radius r, graphing on the t-y plane, and algebraic identity proofs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: General-Angle Definitions and All Six Trigonometric Functions
nodes.explanation: Builds on the unit-circle definition of sine and cosine to define all six trigonometric functions for any angle θ in standard position using an arbitrary point P(x, y) ≠ (0, 0) on the terminal ray at distance r = √(x² + y²): sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, csc θ = r/y, sec θ = r/x, and cot θ = x/y, proving radius-independence via similar triangles scaling P onto the unit circle. Determines exact domains and undefined quadrantal angles (odd multiples of π/2 for tan and sec; integer multiples of π for cot and csc), interprets tan θ geometrically as the slope of the terminal ray, and establishes the quadrant sign patterns for all six functions. Trains the two-step reference-angle evaluation procedure (find the acute reference angle θ' to the nearest x-axis—never the y-axis—and attach the quadrant sign) to compute exact values of all six functions at arbitrary special angles, as well as recovering the remaining five exact values given one ratio and a quadrant condition (using either a signed terminal-ray triangle or the basic reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean relations). Maintains the explicit boundary that reciprocal, quotient, and Pythagorean relations are used here solely for numerical value recovery and definition consistency, leaving algebraic identity verification and manipulation to Trigonometric Identities and Equations.

nodes.label: Graphs of Basic Sine and Cosine Functions
nodes.explanation: Builds on the unit-circle definition of sine and cosine and assumes entry background in function language (domain, range, intercepts, local extrema, and even/odd graph symmetry) to transition from circular coordinates to real-valued graphs on the Cartesian plane. Unwraps the vertical coordinate y = sin x and horizontal coordinate y = cos x as the radian input x varies across [0, 2π] and repeats periodically across ℝ, establishing the five-key-point quarter-period skeleton (0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π) of zeros, maxima, and minima. Identifies domain ℝ, range [−1, 1], fundamental period 2π, amplitude 1, midline y = 0, odd symmetry of sine (origin symmetry), even symmetry of cosine (y-axis symmetry), and the horizontal shift relationship cos x = sin(x + π/2) read directly from the unit circle and graphs. Explicitly cautions against connecting key points with straight V-shaped segments instead of smooth curves with horizontal tangents at extrema. Enables the learner to sketch accurate multi-period graphs of y = sin x and y = cos x and read key features (zeros, extrema, intervals of increase/decrease, and periodicity) directly from the wave. Leaves amplitude, period, midline, and phase-shift transformations to the next lesson.

nodes.label: Amplitude, Period, Phase Shift, and Midline Transformations
nodes.explanation: Builds on the basic sine and cosine graphs and assumes entry background in general function transformations (vertical/horizontal stretches, shifts, and reflections) to analyze and graph general sinusoids y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D and y = A cos(B(x − C)) + D (with A, B ≠ 0). Connects each parameter directly to geometry: amplitude |A|, midline y = D, range [D − |A|, D + |A|], period T = 2π/|B|, vertical reflection when A < 0, and horizontal phase shift C (handling B < 0 cleanly via even/odd symmetry before reading shifts). Highlights the essential algebraic factoring bridge Bx − φ = B(x − φ/B) to prevent the classic mistake of reading φ instead of φ/B as the phase shift. Trains both directions: sketching accurate graphs via the transformed five-key-point method (partitioning one period [C, C + T] into four equal quarter-period steps of length T/4) and writing sinusoidal equations from a given graph (recognizing that the same wave admits multiple equivalent sine and cosine formulas differing in phase shift or sign of A). Enables the learner to move fluently between sinusoidal formulas, parameters, and graphs. Leaves real-world periodic modeling and reciprocal/quotient graphs to subsequent lessons.

nodes.label: Modeling Periodic Phenomena with Sinusoidal Functions
nodes.explanation: Builds on sinusoidal transformations to construct, interpret, and evaluate mathematical models of real-world periodic processes such as Ferris-wheel heights, ocean tides, seasonal daylight or temperature cycles, and idealized harmonic oscillation. Develops the modeling workflow from verbal descriptions or tables of extrema: extracting midline D = (max + min)/2, amplitude |A| = (max − min)/2, period T from full-cycle or half-cycle (peak-to-trough) time spacing to get B = 2π/T, and selecting sine vs. cosine (with positive or negative A) to minimize or eliminate phase shift based on the initial condition at t = 0. Emphasizes interpreting each parameter with physical units, predicting output values at specified times, and identifying when maxima, minima, or midline crossings occur directly from quarter-period symmetry. Explicitly respects the seam boundary by leaving algebraic solving of A sin(B(t − C)) + D = k for arbitrary intermediate target values k to Trigonometric Identities and Equations. Enables the learner to build and interrogate realistic sinusoidal models from physical data.

nodes.label: Graphs of Tangent, Cotangent, Secant, and Cosecant
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes general-angle definitions of all six trigonometric functions (including exact domain exclusions) with sinusoidal transformations to analyze and sketch graphs of y = A tan(B(x − C)) + D, y = A cot(B(x − C)) + D, y = A sec(B(x − C)) + D, and y = A csc(B(x − C)) + D. Develops y = tan x and y = cot x with fundamental period π (emphasizing the frequent error of using 2π/|B| instead of π/|B|), locating consecutive vertical asymptotes (by solving Bx − φ = ±π/2 for tan and 0, π for cot), midpoint zeros/inflection points, and quarter-period guide points at D ± A, noting the range is all of ℝ and that |A| acts as a vertical stretch rather than an amplitude. Develops y = A sec(B(x − C)) + D and y = A csc(B(x − C)) + D via the reciprocal guide-curve bridge: first lightly sketching the corresponding cosine or sine curve, placing vertical asymptotes at its midline crossings, anchoring U-shaped branches at its local extrema, and determining exact range (−∞, D − |A|] ∪ [D + |A|, ∞) and period 2π/|B|. Enables the learner to determine domains, ranges, periods, asymptotes, and graphs for all four remaining trigonometric functions and recover equations from basic transformed graphs.

nodes.label: Triangle Area Formula and the Law of Sines (Unambiguous Cases)
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes solving right triangles with the unit-circle sine of obtuse angles (specifically sin(180° − θ) = sin θ > 0) to extend trigonometry from right triangles to arbitrary oblique triangles. Drops an altitude inside (acute case) or outside (obtuse case) triangle ABC to prove both the SAS area formula K = ½ab sin C (and cyclic permutations) and the Law of Sines (sin A)/a = (sin B)/b = (sin C)/c by equating altitude expressions (or dividing K = ½ab sin C = ½bc sin A = ½ac sin B by ½abc). Applies the Law of Sines to solve the unique AAS and ASA triangle cases (first finding the third angle via angle sum 180°, then computing both unknown sides while retaining exact intermediate expressions), checks that larger angles lie opposite longer sides, and uses the area formula for triangles and polygons partitioned into triangles. Explicitly defers the SSA (side-side-angle) case—where solving for an angle via sine can produce zero, one, or two triangles—to the immediately following lesson so learners first master the Law of Sines in its unambiguous setting.

nodes.label: The Ambiguous Case (SSA) of the Law of Sines
nodes.explanation: Builds on the Law of Sines (and uses sin(180° − B) = sin B from the unit circle, with calculator sin⁻¹ supplied strictly as a numerical lookup for acute angles in (0°, 90°)) to resolve the Side-Side-Angle (SSA) configuration. Connects geometry and algebra by comparing the opposite side a against the altitude h = b sin A and adjacent side b: when A is acute, classifying a < h (no triangle), a = h (one right triangle), h < a < b (two distinct triangles—one with acute B₁ and one with obtuse B₂ = 180° − B₁), and a ≥ b (one triangle); when A ≥ 90°, classifying a ≤ b (no triangle) vs. a > b (one triangle). Trains the reliable algebraic-geometric workflow: compute sin B = (b sin A)/a; if sin B > 1 conclude no triangle; otherwise take acute B₁ = sin⁻¹((b sin A)/a), test whether its supplement B₂ = 180° − B₁ satisfies A + B₂ < 180°, and solve both complete triangles whenever both are valid. Guards against the common error of stopping after the calculator's acute output B₁ and silently dropping the valid obtuse-triangle solution. Enables the learner to determine the exact number of triangles for any SSA data and compute all valid solutions.

nodes.label: The Law of Cosines
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes solving right triangles with unit-circle sine and cosine of obtuse angles (specifically cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ and cos² C + sin² C = 1) to derive and apply the Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C (and its cyclic forms). Proves the law cleanly for acute, right, and obtuse angles C at once by placing vertex C at the origin, A at (b, 0), and B at (a cos C, a sin C) and applying the Pythagorean distance relation, noting that C = 90° recovers the Pythagorean theorem while the sign of cos C distinguishes acute (c² < a² + b²) from obtuse (c² > a² + b²) angles. Supplies calculator cos⁻¹ strictly as a numerical lookup on (0°, 180°), highlighting the crucial structural contrast with the Law of Sines: because cosine is strictly decreasing across (0°, 180°) (positive for acute angles, negative for obtuse angles), cos⁻¹ uniquely determines any triangle angle with no SSA-style ambiguity. Trains solving SAS triangles (finding the opposite side first) and SSS triangles (verifying the triangle inequality a + b > c, solving for the largest angle first so any remaining angles are guaranteed acute, and avoiding sign errors when subtracting a negative product −2ab cos C). Enables the learner to solve any valid SAS or SSS triangle and diagnose impossible SSS data.

nodes.label: Choosing Triangle-Solving Strategies and Applied Geometry
nodes.explanation: Synthesizes the Law of Sines (including the ambiguous SSA case), the Law of Cosines, and the SAS triangle area formula into a complete decision framework for oblique-triangle geometry and real-world applications. Trains classifying given data (AAS, ASA, SSA, SAS, SSS) to select the right starting law, managing hybrid multi-step calculations safely—especially avoiding the classic trap of solving an SAS triangle with the Law of Cosines and then blindly applying the Law of Sines to the largest remaining angle (instead finding the smaller remaining angle via Law of Sines or continuing with Law of Cosines)—and verifying consistency via angle sum and side-angle order. Applies the full toolkit to navigation and compass-bearing courses (heading/distance after two legs), surveying across obstacles, triangulation from two baseline stations, and finding unknown diagonals or areas of irregular quadrilaterals. Enables the learner to choose and execute complete, ambiguity-free triangle-solving strategies on multi-step applied problems.

nodes.label: Heron's Formula for Triangle Area
nodes.explanation: Optional enrichment synthesizing the SAS area formula K = ½ab sin C with the Law of Cosines to derive and apply Heron's formula K = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)), where s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semiperimeter. Develops the algebraic derivation bridge via K² = ¼a²b²(1 − cos² C) = ¼a²b²(1 − cos C)(1 + cos C), substituting cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab) and factoring differences of squares—giving learners a complete secondary-level proof that requires no calculus or advanced identities while illustrating how the triangle inequality ensures every factor s − a, s − b, s − c is positive. Applies Heron's formula to compute areas of SSS triangles directly without solving for an intermediate angle and to measure areas of irregular polygonal land parcels partitioned into triangles.
